The 2026 Escalation in the Middle East: A Data Analysis of ACLED Conflict Data (2025–2026)¶

Course: Data Science Basics – Project Hand-in

Project summary¶

This project looks at political violence and protests in the Middle East during 2026. It uses 2025 as a baseline for comparison. 2026 began with a wave of deadly unrest in Iran. From the end of February, the data shows a sharp increase in air, drone and missile strikes. These strikes also reached the Gulf states, which had recorded almost no such events before. Using weekly conflict data, the notebook measures when the escalation started, where it happened, how the type of violence changed, and how deadly the different kinds of events were.

Data source¶

  • ACLED – Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, Middle East aggregated data (weekly, by first-level administrative region), data up to the week of 2026-11-07. Downloaded from https://acleddata.com (Data Export Tool → Aggregated data), November 2026.
  • Citation: Raleigh, C., Linke, A., Hegre, H. & Karlsen, J. (2010). Introducing ACLED: An Armed Conflict Location and Event Dataset. Journal of Peace Research, 47(5), 651–660.
  • The full file has 156,865 rows from 2015 to 2026. This analysis uses the 31,288 rows from January 2025 to November 2026.
  • Each row is one combination of week × country × province (ADMIN1) × event type × sub-event type and gives the number of EVENTS and reported FATALITIES.

Note on fatalities: ACLED fatality numbers are conservative estimates based on reports, so they are not exact counts. When ACLED cannot assign deaths to individual days, it sometimes records large numbers in a single week.

Research questions¶

  1. Timing: How did weekly conflict events and fatalities develop in 2026 compared with 2025, and when did the escalation start?
  2. Countries: Which countries were most affected in 2026, and how does this compare with 2025?
  3. Iran: How did the type of conflict in Iran change during 2026?
  4. Spillover: Did the conflict spread to the Gulf states (Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia), and when?
  5. Lethality: Which types of events were the deadliest (fatalities per event) in 2026 compared with 2025?

Data preparation¶

  • Keep only weeks from 2025-01-01 onwards.
  • Add YEAR and WEEK_NO (week 1 = first week of the year). The data ends at week 45 of 2026, so all year-to-year comparisons use weeks 1–45 of both years. This keeps the comparison fair. All 2026 data is used. Only 2025 is shortened to the same weeks.
  • POPULATION_EXPOSURE has missing values, but none of the five questions use it, so it is left as it is.
In [4]:
df = raw[raw["WEEK"] >= "2025-01-01"].copy()
df["YEAR"] = df["WEEK"].dt.year
df["WEEK_NO"] = df.groupby("YEAR")["WEEK"].transform(lambda w: (w - w.min()).dt.days // 7 + 1)

N_WEEKS = df.loc[df["YEAR"] == 2026, "WEEK_NO"].max()
cmp_ = df[df["WEEK_NO"] <= N_WEEKS]          # comparable period: weeks 1..N_WEEKS of each year

print("Rows used (2025–2026):", len(df))
print("Comparable weeks per year:", N_WEEKS)
print("Missing values:\n", df.isna().sum()[lambda s: s > 0])
cmp_.groupby("YEAR")[["EVENTS", "FATALITIES"]].sum()

2. Q1 – When did the escalation start?¶

The chart shows weekly totals for the whole region, with 2026 compared against the same weeks of 2025. Events and fatalities are on very different scales, so they are drawn as two separate charts instead of one chart with two y-axes. The fatality chart uses a log scale so that one extreme week does not hide all the others.

In [5]:

yearly = cmp_.groupby("YEAR")[["EVENTS", "FATALITIES"]].sum()
print(yearly.assign(EV_change=yearly["EVENTS"].pct_change(), FAT_change=yearly["FATALITIES"].pct_change()))

Answer Q1¶

In weeks 1–45, the region recorded 26% more events in 2026 than in the same weeks of 2025 (72,404 vs. 57,324) and 63% more reported fatalities (48,575 vs. 29,794). These figures compare like with like. The data ends in week 45 of 2026, so 2025 is also limited to weeks 1–45. As a robustness check, comparing 2026 with all 52 weeks of 2025 still gives +12% events and +57% fatalities (64,561 → 72,404 and 30,886 → 48,575), even though 2026 has 7 fewer weeks of data. The conclusion does not depend on this choice. The escalation has a clear starting point: the week of 28 February 2026. During the first eight weeks of 2026, activity was actually below 2025 levels (about 1,120 events per week). It then jumped to 2,764 events in a single week and peaked at 2,912 events in the week of 7 March. Over weeks 9–14 the average was about 2,700 events per week, roughly 2.4 times the level before the escalation. By mid-April activity was back at 2025 levels. A second rise started in September, peaking in the week of 3 October (2,252 events, 1,371 fatalities), and stayed well above 2025 until November. The fatality curve looks different. The deadliest week is 3 January 2026, when about 27,700 fatalities were recorded, mainly during unrest in Iran. That single week makes up 57% of all 2026 fatalities. Without it, 2026 (about 20,900) would actually have fewer recorded fatalities than 2025, when the war in Gaza was still very deadly.

Totals for weeks 1–45 of each year. The two maritime areas (Mediterranean Sea and Indian Ocean) are left out because they are not countries.

summary.sort_values("events_2026", ascending=False)

Answer Q2¶

The countries most affected changed noticeably between the two years:

  • Lebanon had 4.2 times more events (3,234 → 13,498) and about 8 times more fatalities (371 → 3,054).
  • Iran had 2.8 times more events (4,002 → 11,047), and its fatalities rose from 1,293 to 29,695. That makes Iran the country with the most fatalities in 2026.
  • Yemen had about the same number of events (around 11,000), but its fatalities more than quadrupled (2,607 → 11,435).
  • Palestine still had the most events (14,769), but its fatalities fell sharply (16,453 → 1,709). Syria's fatalities also fell, from 8,461 to 1,810.
  • The Gulf states went from almost nothing to measurable activity. For example, the UAE went from 4 to 228 events, Saudi Arabia from 19 to 415, and Oman from 1 to 104. Kuwait had no events in 2025 and 313 in 2026.

In short, the centre of the conflict moved from Gaza and Syria (2025) towards Iran, Lebanon and Yemen (2026).

Answer Q3¶

In 2025, most recorded events in Iran were protests (3,656 of 4,581 events). The main exception was a short burst of strikes in June 2025. In 2026, Iran went through two very different phases:

  1. January – a protest and riot wave. In the week of 3 January there were 385 protests and 172 riots. ACLED records about 27,500 fatalities for that week, almost all under Riots (22,673 for the year) and Protests (4,953). These categories describe how the participants behaved, not who caused the deaths. In ACLED's definitions, Riots are demonstrations where participants themselves become violent (sub-type Violent demonstration) or Mob violence. Protests are non-violent demonstrations, and the only protest sub-type that can involve deaths is Excessive force against protesters, meaning lethal force used by authorities against peaceful demonstrators. Most of the deaths recorded in January were therefore most likely demonstrators killed while the protests were being suppressed, rather than people killed by rioters. After that, activity almost stopped (fewer than 10 events per week in mid-January).
  2. From 28 February – a strike campaign. Explosions/Remote violence (air and drone strikes, missiles, shelling) went from about 0 to more than 500 events per week for six weeks. In total there were 3,596 such events in 2026, compared with 459 in 2025. Protests also continued during this time (200–320 per week).

From April the strikes decreased, with smaller bursts in the summer, and by autumn the pattern was mostly protests again. The conflict in Iran changed from domestic unrest into an external military escalation.

5. Q4 – Did the conflict spill over into the Gulf states?¶

Monthly number of Explosions/Remote violence events (air/drone strikes, missile attacks, shelling and similar) in the six Gulf Cooperation Council states, shown as a heatmap. Months with no recorded events show as 0.

GULF = ["Saudi Arabia", "United Arab Emirates", "Kuwait", "Bahrain", "Qatar", "Oman"]
g = df[df["COUNTRY"].isin(GULF) & (df["EVENT_TYPE"] == "Explosions/Remote violence")]
months = pd.period_range("2025-01", df["WEEK"].max().to_period("M"), freq="M")
heat = (g.pivot_table(index="COUNTRY", columns=g["WEEK"].dt.to_period("M"), values="EVENTS", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
          .reindex(index=GULF, columns=months, fill_value=0))
print("Explosions/Remote violence events per year:\n", g.pivot_table(index="COUNTRY", columns="YEAR", values="EVENTS", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0))
print("\nFirst 2026 week with such events per country:\n", g[g.YEAR == 2026].groupby("COUNTRY")["WEEK"].min())

ax.grid(which="minor", color="white", linewidth=2); ax.grid(which="major", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)
for s in ax.spines.values(): s.set_visible(False)
for i in range(heat.shape[0]):
    for j in range(heat.shape[1]):
        v = heat.values[i, j]
        if v > 0:
            ax.text(j, i, int(v), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                    color="white" if v > heat.values.max() * 0.45 else "#0b0b0b")
cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, pad=0.01); cb.set_label("Events per month"); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("Q4 · Gulf states: monthly explosions / remote-violence events, 2025–2026", fontsize=14)
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "q4_gulf_heatmap")

Answer Q4¶

Yes. In 2025, the six Gulf states recorded only 6 explosions/remote-violence events in total (Saudi Arabia 4, Qatar 2). In 2026 they recorded 486: Kuwait 118, UAE 105, Saudi Arabia 91, Oman 90, Bahrain 56 and Qatar 26. The timing is very clear. All six countries recorded their first such event of 2026 in the same week, 28 February 2026, which is the same week the strikes began in Iran. The peak was in March 2026 (UAE 53, Kuwait 49 events). After that the countries developed differently. The UAE, Bahrain and Qatar returned to almost zero by May to July. Kuwait had another spike in July. Saudi Arabia and Oman had a second wave in September and October (28 events each in October), which matches the regional rise seen in Q1. The number of fatalities in the Gulf stayed low (for example, Saudi Arabia 38, Oman 19). This suggests the spillover mostly involved strikes that were intercepted or did little damage, rather than heavy fighting.

6. Q5 – Which event types were the deadliest?¶

Lethality is measured as fatalities per event for each ACLED event type (weeks 1–45 of each year). The one week in Iran beginning 3 January 2026 contains about 27,500 of the year's recorded fatalities. It is therefore also shown excluded as a sensitivity check, to see how much this single week changes the result.

In [13]:
def lethality(d):
    t = d.groupby("EVENT_TYPE")[["EVENTS", "FATALITIES"]].sum()
    return t["FATALITIES"] / t["EVENTS"]

iran_jan = (cmp_["COUNTRY"] == "Iran") & (cmp_["WEEK"] == "2026-01-03")
leth = pd.DataFrame({
    "2025": lethality(cmp_[cmp_["YEAR"] == 2025]),
    "2026": lethality(cmp_[cmp_["YEAR"] == 2026]),
    "2026 excl. Iran week of 3 Jan": lethality(cmp_[(cmp_["YEAR"] == 2026) & ~iran_jan]),
}).reindex(TYPES[::-1])
print("Fatalities in Iran week of 3 Jan 2026:", cmp_.loc[iran_jan, "FATALITIES"].sum())
leth.round(3)

Answer Q5¶

Measured as fatalities per event:

  • 2025: the deadliest types were Explosions/Remote violence (1.32), Battles (1.28) and Violence against civilians (1.08). Protests and riots were almost never deadly.
  • 2026 (all data): Riots show the highest value (3.28), followed by Battles (2.20). However, the sensitivity check shows that the riot result comes entirely from the single Iranian week of 3 January. Without that week, riots and protests drop back to about 0.01. Riots therefore do not lead to deaths by their nature. ACLED records an event as a riot when the demonstrators are violent. Deaths recorded in these events can still be caused by security forces responding to them (see Q3).
  • Without that week, Battles are clearly the deadliest event type in 2026 (2.20 fatalities per event), and their lethality increased compared with 2025.
  • Explosions/Remote violence rose from 13,653 to 24,527 events, but their lethality fell from 1.32 to 0.41. The 2026 strikes were much more frequent but less deadly per event than the strikes of 2025, which were concentrated in Gaza.

This question also shows that one extreme value can strongly change a summary statistic, so it is important to check whether a result depends on a single outlier.

7. Bonus – Where did the fatalities happen in 2026?¶

A geographic bubble chart (scatter plot of province centroids by longitude and latitude). Bubble size shows reported fatalities in 2026 (the bubble area grows with the square root of fatalities, so that Tehran does not cover the whole map), and the colour shows the country group. It summarises the four questions above on one map.

8. Conclusion¶

The ACLED data shows that 2026 was a year of escalation in the Middle East: 26% more events and 63% more reported fatalities than in the same weeks of 2025. The escalation came in two stages. First, a deadly wave of unrest in Iran in early January. Then, from 28 February 2026, a sudden regional strike campaign. This campaign more than doubled weekly events across the region, turned Iran into a target of air and drone strikes, and spread to all six Gulf states in the same week. At the same time, the centre of the conflict moved away from Gaza and Syria and towards Iran, Lebanon and Yemen. The analysis also shows that the 2026 fatality figures depend heavily on one extreme week. Without that week, 2026 had more events than 2025 but fewer fatalities.

Limitations: ACLED counts reported events, so the coverage depends on media access. This is especially true in Iran and Yemen. Fatality figures are estimates, and a single week can include deaths that happened over several days. Whether a demonstration is coded as a protest (non-violent participants) or a riot (violent participants) is decided by ACLED's coders, based on how the sources describe it. Where media access is restricted, such as in Iran, this classification is less certain. The aggregated data also does not show who the actors were, so the results describe what happened and where, but not who was responsible.
